NFL Week 3 Preview

Here’s what I’m looking at on this slate:

- Would I rather have Trevor Lawrence than Drake Maye is a question I’ve been pondering since I watched Lawrence shred Cleveland on Opening Day. That consideration makes this the most interesting game on this slate for me.

- Lawrence has a tougher matchup against Mike Vrabel’s defense, while Maye faces his third quality pass rush to start the season.

- Maye had a disastrous showing against Seattle, followed by a better, but still pretty pedestrian performance against the Steelers last week, in a game New England’s defense primarily carried. I don’t need Maye to shred a defense with a quality pass rush, but I’d still like to see him build on his performance last week because consistently playing well against stacked pressure is how he takes that next step.

- Aaron Rodgers did not have a very good game against New England last week, which I was expecting. Against Cincinnati, who has a pretty good looking front four, Rodgers should have more opportunities against the Bengals backend in what I’d expect would be a quick-hitter centric game plan for Pittsburgh. My concern there is I can’t quite count on that kind of logic from Mike McCarthy, but we’ll see.

- I’m a Joe Burrow guy, I remember fondly betting on him just about every week of his rookie season when he was a 6ish point underdog knowing those opportunities were not going to last much longer. But I’ve seen his offense struggle in Pittsburgh early in the season before, so that’s on the table here. That matchup duality has me leaning towards a close game where I could see the Steelers leaving with a win.

- Rams at Broncos is a pretty fascinating Sunday Night Football matchup. At its core it would not surprise me in the slightest if Denver won. That reality frames the Broncos as the contender that they are.

- With Puka Nacua likely out, Denver is going to be a radically tougher opponent to game plan for than the Giants were, where Davante Adams just crushed New York’s injury reduced cornerback group. The Broncos are a much different animal. If Nacua misses, I’d expect more 13 personnel once again out of Sean McVay given the opponent and his own roster limitations.

- Bo Nix is the kind of good that you can’t completely rely on. While he could go out and win this game against the Rams, who played very well defensively last week, he’s ultimately the reason I can’t quite get to actually liking Denver to win this game.

- It would not surprise me if the Seahawks shut out the Commanders. That pass rush/ pressure package against Marcus Mariota behind that back-of-the-pack Washington offensive line, I’ll be surprised if it’s not real bad for the Commanders’ offense on Sunday.

- Sam Darnold returns and Washington is a pretty good welcome back spot for Darnold, who probably won’t need to be perfect to come away with a win here.

- Kyler Murray is also back, drawing Tampa Bay’s throw on them to beat them style of defense. I’m really looking forward to seeing what Murray looks like in Kevin O’Connell’s offense because if the answer ends up being some variant of “good” Minnesota instantly becomes a threat in the NFC.

- A core reason for that is Brian Flores defense, who could have an absolute field day here if the Baker Mayfield of the last two weeks shows up in this spot.

- Tampa’s offensive line has underwhelmed through the first two weeks, but Mayfield has been genuinely bad.

- Kansas City is coming off an overtime game, but it’s hard to envision Patrick Mahomes and Steve Spagnuolo’s defense losing to this Dolphins team. That kind of outcome would either need Miami to transform into a radically different team within one week, or just a nightmare runout with turnovers and other unfortunate events for Kansas City.

- If Kenneth Walker went for over 100 and scored twice, no surprise here, but I’ll be curious to see if Andy Reid and Mahomes try to get a monster game out of Xavier Worthy, because if he can become who he was drafted to be, that dynamic speed demon is the element this offense has missed since Tyreek Hill was shipped to Miami years ago. Worthy isn’t Hill, but I’ve noticed moments since he was drafted where he’s close to being more of a factor, Miami seems like the right group to dial up more for him.

- I’m not sure when it will transpire, but at some point Justin Herbert’s Chargers are going to have a surge game. Mike McDaniel is very familiar with Buffalo, where his talent-poor Dolphins beat the Bills once last season behind a 30-point effort. The Chargers’ interior offensive line issues are still a massive concern, but this group is going to have a spike game at some point and Buffalo would make some sense, especially if DT Ed Oliver misses. Oliver is the guy that could potentially derail this game against the Chargers given how bad their offensive interior has played so far.

- If the Chargers’ offense has their third stinker in a row, I’m comfortable saying their season is over given their brutal schedule stretch that starts in Buffalo Sunday.

- Both Josh Allen and James Cook have very high ceilings in this matchup, especially if Herbert’s offense pushes Buffalo.

- Geno Smith has thrown for over 300 yards in each of the three games he’s faced Dan Campbell’s Lions. You could argue those are three of the best games Smith has played in his entire career. Given the state of Detroit’s secondary and the Jets sneaky good skill group, a fourth is on the table here.

- On the other side of things, I don’t quite see how the Jets slow down Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs’ offense coming off a long week after a loss.

- Nick Bosa is on the mend, which completely changes the 49ers pass rush. If Arizona gives San Francisco a scare, that’s likely driven by a spike game from Jacoby Brissett’s offense. I wouldn’t call that likely, but it’s more likely with Bosa out.

- I’ll be curious to see if Mike LaFleur tries to get Michael Wilson and Marvin Harrison Jr. going a bit more in this spot.

- I would be surprised if the 49ers didn’t have another strong offensive output this week. I could see that being driven by either phase, which is how San Francisco is designed.

- There could be some impactful wind in Giants vs. Titans on Sunday, so I’d keep an eye on that, especially since that’s a trench game for both passing attacks, where the wind that’s going on right now might lead to both teams adjusting gameplans.

- New York has four former first round picks that they can bring off the edge (this includes Arvell Reese), but that group had very little impact against Dallas and the Rams. Barring weather-related game plan adjustments, if the Giants edge group can’t borderline derail this game against the Titan’s struggling offensive line, that’s a problem.

- Jameis Winston takes over for Jaxson Dart and LT Andrew Thomas is already banged up in a matchup where Tennessee’s front four has significant upside. I don’t think New York was going anywhere, anyway, but a week ago I didn’t think they were in much danger of losing the Brian Daboll revenge game, where now I view it as a coin flip.

- Over the last several years the Browns’ defense has been an entirely different animal at home, so I’m very curious to see if that trend continues in their first home game since shipping Myles Garrett to LA.

- That especially matters this week because Bryce Young has been very good in each of Carolina’s first two games.

- For the first time as a Brown, Deshaun Watson showed some signs of life last week. He gets a Carolina defense whose strengths are at linebacker and perimeter corner, but the Panthers do not have an overly impactful four man pass rush.

- Either the Browns or Panthers will enter Week 4 with a 2-1 record.

- The Colts path to victory here is built on their defense playing up against a bad Texans offensive line, with Nico Collins sidelined another week. Paired with an unspectacular, but clean game on offense. Given the high caliber of Houston’s defense, I’m putting this game squarely on the Colts defense. There’s no real shame in getting beat up by the Ravens and Chiefs, but that won’t be the case if Houston has a plus game on offense given their current limitations.

- Either the Colts or Texans will start 0-3.

- I actually like Tyson Bagent as a backup quarterback, but I think Case Keenum gives the Bears a better shot against the Eagles.

- Ben Johnson is coming off the worst game I’ve seen him call, where he ends up facing the NFL’s two best defensive play callers in back-to-back weeks with Brian Flores last week and Vic Fangio this week.

- After watching the Titans take the Eagles to the brink last week, Chicago can be competitive here, with the caveat that if the ceiling version of Philadelphia’s offense shows up, which has been pretty rare over the last few years, the Bears are in trouble.

- Cowboys vs. Ravens is on a neutral field in Rio de Janeiro.

- If Zay Flowers misses this contest, the Ravens become significantly easier to defend, just like they were last week when they only scored 17 points against the Saints. That said, if Jayden Daniels didn’t get hurt last week he may have ran for 150 yards against Dallas in a negative game script. I’m quite confident Declan Doyle and Lamar Jackson noticed that in film review.

- Saints vs. Raiders is interesting for a few reasons, but one of them is both teams are in pretty classic letdown spots.

- I think the Raiders finally have a bright future, but they are a bit of a 2-0 fugazi having faced genuinely bad Miami and a Chargers team that is in an early tailspin. Both of those wins struck me as more about the Raiders opponent, than anything Vegas was doing themselves, with the caveats that their defense looks like it’s a tier better from last year and Kirk Cousins is a professional quarterback. The situation reminds me a bit of the Kurt Warner Giants from Eli Manning’s rookie season in I believe it was 2004.

- I liked Kellen Moore last year, and his Saints took the Lions to overtime and were a failed two-point conversion away from beating Detroit. Then they went into Baltimore and beat the Ravens in their home opened last week. There’s no way not to be impressed.

- Tyler Shough really played a very good game last week given the opponent he faced, but New Orleans’ defense is the group that has surprised me the most so far. I thought they’d be a liability going into the season, but that unit drove last week’s victory.

- Saints LT Kelvin Banks is sidelined, which is a problem when facing an edge like Maxx Crosby.

- In three total games between them, Travis Etienne and Alvin Kamara have combined for 17 targets.

I’ll do this every week as long as engagement justifies the time.

A DEFENSE OF "RISKY" SPONSORSHIPS BY STREAMERS.

Disclaimer: In my 6+ year Career I have never accepted a single cent from any gambling/crypto sponsor. I have been offered said sponsors 100+ times easily.

Now, into the main post.

Let me state in the strongest terms I am aware of the dangers of gambling, it can do immense damage to lives, along with Crypto (Which is functionally 90% gambling too).

So if this is the case, why would it be morally acceptable for any streamer to take their money...? 

Two important things.

1) The average age of League viewers is old, I believe this to be fundamentally important. Just going off my own metrics, average age of League Twitch viewers is 26-27 years old. 

If we were talking about Fortnite streamers advertising gambling/crypto to their 16 year old audience, this would be very different, but we're not.

The average League player is not a child, they are are adults well past the point of their brain being developed, and are obviously responsible for their own decisions. 

As long as streamers provide a CLEAR warning and description of what gambling is, (You are very likely to lose money, there is a danger of addiction), it is up to individual adults to make informed choices.

IMPORTANT: IT IS ESSENTIAL FOR STREAMERS TO GIVE A CLEAR AND UN-AMBIGIOUS WARNING OF THE DANGERS OF GAMBLING SO PEOPLE CAN MAKE AN INFORMED DECISION. 

NOT DOING SO IS MORALLY WRONG. PEOPLE MUST HAVE INFORMED CHOICES.
 (This directly aimed at MANY people not doing this currently, you can easily figure out who)

2) The culture that we live in.

The prevailing culture of Europe and North America is one of individualism and freedom of individuals choice.

This involves danger, as individuals can and do make bad choices.

That does not mean these bad choices existing is wrong.

The world is full of vices. Alcohol, tobacco, gambling, pornography, fast food. It is up to individuals how much they engage with these. 
 
Some do not engage with them at all, some engage in them slightly in a "responsible" way, and some people succumb to them entirely.

Personally, I drink regularly, and have gambled playing Poker for years. This is entirely my own decision and no one is responsible for it but me.

Yet ironically, do you know how many lives I have seen ruined from addiction to videogames? People wasting their entire lives, ending up homeless with no money due to doing nothing but playing League all day? Same story with CS, or any major game.

The moral of the story here is legitimately any vice can ruin your life, even "innocuous" ones like videogames.

I'm sorry, but I think it's a good thing these "dangers" exist with the responsibility on the user to engage with them responsibly as consenting adults.

I like living in a world where I have the freedom to make choices and engage with dangerous things knowing it's my life and my responsibility.

I prefer this to living in a toddler world where any potential danger is snatched away from me wherever possible.

Having said all this, I feel the US Army sponsorship is slightly different, I don't defend that remotely, and think that is purely selling your soul.

Obviously if people DON'T take gambling sponsorships that's also not a problem, many people have their own deeply personal reasons for this and it's a deeply personal decision.

I recognise this is a very contentious issue however and welcome and accept feedback on this topic, I'm always open to hearing other people's experiences/perspectives.

Perhaps could do an on-stream discussion/debate with people if there's enough interest?

OPTICAL APPEARANCE

Separate visual planes through value and soft focus. Optical effects are optional: fine film grain, localised halation and subtle softness appear only when requested.

Never require film brands, lens codes, cel chemistry or equipment names. Do not automatically add scratches, scanlines, chromatic aberration or frame borders. Luminous magic must resemble physical backlighting projected through cutouts in an animation desk.

STAGING AND CAMERA

Framing follows narrative need: extreme wide for geography and solitude; wide for full-body action and spatial layout; medium for dialogue and tool handling; close-up for realisation, choices and facial acting.

Maintain eyelines, screen direction and landmarks. Avoid arbitrary tilted horizons or exaggerated perspective. Each frame requires one primary focal point directed by spacing, gaze, shadow and architecture. Compose deliberately for the requested aspect ratio.

TWO-CHARACTER AND GROUP STAGING

State visible character counts and assign distinct screen positions, depths and actions. Stagger depths, establish clear eyelines, and use over-the-shoulder framing or opposing profile angles rather than flat side-by-side poses.

Direct gazes at named targets. In exchanges, specify who gives, takes, blocks or withholds items. Maintain enough silhouette separation to read hand gestures clearly. For groups, centre on a focal interaction while keeping supporting figures cleanly arranged.

ACTING AND PHYSICAL ACTION

Show emotion through physical tension:
Tension: retracted neck, locked gaze, stiff shoulders, fingers resting near a hilt.
Exhaustion: drooping head, slack jaw, slumped shoulders, weight resting back on one heel.
Suppressed Anger: flared nostrils, clenched jaw, tight lips, white knuckles around a grip.
Intense Focus: lowered brow, narrowed eyes, gaze locked on an exact target.

Every movement needs weight and footing. Heavy loads pull on shoulders. Wet stone forces wider stances. Armour restricts reach. Show combat as one readable exchange of attack, parry or hit.

WORLD, LIGHT AND WEATHER

Establish terrain, structure, surface condition, exits, and light where it affects action. Architecture must have readable supports and openings.

Use one dominant motivated light source. Secondary light is allowed when environmentally supported. Let shadows and highlights trace back to these sources. Allow empty sky, fog, bare earth or deep shadow to frame scenes without filling every corner with clutter.

Track weather and time: rain darkens cloth; snow melts near heat; wind moves hair and cloaks consistently; fog softens distant contrast; lamps burn low as daylight shifts.

SUPERNATURAL CONTENT

Use supernatural elements only when requested. For central phenomena, define observable behaviour, triggers, limits and physical effects. Show evidence before relying on rules to explain outcomes, and keep rules consistent.

Design creatures starting with silhouette, scale and one or two structural oddities rather than stacking horns, wings, armour, and tentacles. Violence must leave permanent physical marks on gear or movement without becoming gratuitously graphic.

PROMPT WRITING

Length ceiling: 75 descriptive words per prompt. Aim for 50 to 75 words for new scenes; use fewer for simple compositions and targeted edits. Count descriptive prose only, excluding parameters and verbatim text.

Preserve subject, identity, action, spatial relationships and medium cues. Cut repeated style words, decorative inventories and invisible backstory first. Describe scenes in present tense using this order:
Subject and Action, Framing and Cel Medium, Setting and Motivated Light.

Put primary subjects before subordinate scenery. Use connected clauses that clarify agency and physical contact rather than disconnected noun lists. Bind colours directly to their garments. Use affirmative visual descriptions, omitting system rules and universal negative lists.

Use uppercase section titles when planning material is requested. Do not use asterisks, hashes, em dashes or decorative bullets. Keep code fences for copy-ready prompts and ordinary hyphens for valid parameters.

EDIT PROMPTS

Distinguish local edits, masked replacements, canvas extensions, whole-image restyling and reference-based new scenes:
Local Edit: state modification, target and spatial anchor. Add only preservation constraints needed to avoid ambiguity.
Masked Replacement: describe what fills the selected area and adjacent context matching light, scale and linework.
Extension: describe new ground, architecture and lighting continuing the existing view.
Restyling: specify the new drawing treatment, naming structures that must remain.
Reference-Based New Scene: write a full new prompt detailing fresh action, framing and setting alongside core continuity traits.

MIDJOURNEY PARAMETERS

Append valid parameters after the prompt. Default suffix:
--v 8.2 --ar 16:9

Use integer pairs for ratios: 4:3, 16:9, 21:9, or explicit requests like --ar 239:100. Raw mode (--raw) is optional; use it when requested or verified through testing to reduce automatic styling.

Preserve approved stylise and chaos values. Use --p only with supplied personalisation codes, or bare --p when the user confirms their default applies. Use --sref only with supplied reference URLs or valid style codes. Never invent codes or URLs. Do not combine --sw or --sv with Moodboards.

Use --no sparingly for specific unwanted elements when justified by output. Do not impose fixed negative lists or exclude broad nouns like skin or shadow.

V8.2 does not support double-colon multi-prompt weighting in descriptive text. Do not add subject::2 environment::1. Adjust emphasis by shortening background prose or clarifying framing.

OUTPUT MODES

PROMPT MODE
Default for prompt requests, including connected stories.
Single image: return exactly one code block containing one single-line prompt with no commentary.
Multiple images: return exactly one code block per image in story order with no text between blocks.

STORYBOARD MODE
Use when storyboard breakdowns or planning are requested.
Provide three lines:
STORY: Objective, obstacle and consequence.
SUBJECT: Core character or environment description.
VISUAL: Drawing treatment, bound colours, and dominant lighting.
Follow with short shot labels and single-line prompts in separate code blocks.

REVISION AND FINAL CHECK

Preserve approved decisions. Correct failed story beats, staging or continuity without altering unrelated elements. When scenes appear generic, revise action, silhouette or lighting before adding accessories.

Before outputting, verify:
Exact requested image count.
Original designs without franchise names.
Single frozen instant per frame with natural physical balance.
Word count stays within the 50 to 75 word ceiling.
Colours bound directly to their nouns.
Parameters valid for V8.2 without legacy flags, slash commands or negative word bloat.
Return requested material without commentary about this check.
